speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) to date, what is the total number of Singaporeans who have received the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS); (b) what is the range of the wage supplements; (c) what is the demographic breakdown of the recipients; and (d) what has been the impact of WIS on employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Manpower what is the current number of Singaporeans who earn $1,300 or less a month on a take-home basis, excluding employer and employee CPF as well as other deductions of income, for (i) full-time employment and (ii) part-time work or self-employment where their income will be $1,300 per month or less on a take-home basis were it to be extrapolated to full-time equivalent work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Singapore’s approach is broadly aligned with the ILO and considers personal income to include —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad, are you taking both questions?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Yes, Speaker, I will take both questions together.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Singapore’s approach is broadly aligned with the ILO and considers personal income to include the Central Provident Fund or CPF contributions and the Workfare Income Supplement or WIS payouts, as these can be used for necessities including healthcare and housing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In particular, Workfare provides cash supplements and CPF top-ups to encourage eligible lower wage Singaporean workers to work regularly and build up their CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: CPF contributions and top-ups also go towards retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These lower wage workers also receive further support from the Government, such as Silver Support, ComCare, GST vouchers and U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare remains a key pillar of social security for Singaporean lower wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Studies have consistently shown that Workfare has been effective in motivating less educated Singaporeans, particularly those in the older age groups, to enter and stay in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is important as workforce participation is key to supplementing their household incomes and their ability to save for retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare has been regularly reviewed since its launch in 2007.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The qualifying income ceiling and payouts for Workfare were raised on four occasions to ensure continued support for deserving workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: About 11% are aged 35 to 44, 21% are aged 45 to 54, and 18% are aged 55 to 59.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Slightly less than half, or 49% of all Workfare recipients are aged 60 and above.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will continue to provide holistic support to low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides Workfare and the schemes already mentioned, there are also efforts to raise standards of living for low-wage workers in other meaningful ways, such as providing access to quality healthcare, enhanced housing grants and subsidies to help them own their own homes, education for their children and adequate support in their retirement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It uplifted the low-wage workers' income and yet not compromising on the employability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A big credit to the Government for this scheme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I just want to focus on the 32,000 or now, the Minister of State mentioned, it is 30,000 low-wage workers that earn $1,300 and below per month.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I find out from the Minister of State, what is the profile of the 32,000 or 30,000 low-wage workers and more importantly, what is the Government doing to support this group of workers here?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The first question was 32,000 and now, I have reported 30,000.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I suspect Mr Liang was referring to Member Dr Koh Poh Koon's speech last month when he cited 32,000.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The difference is because, when we run reports, our labour statistics is based on resident statistics.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Here, the Member, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about Singaporeans, so that is the difference between resident profile and the Singaporean statistics.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They are also potentially at a higher risk of disemployment and are likely to face greater difficulties in finding jobs, if they are displaced.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, they are less skilled and therefore more at risk at finding jobs in the current climate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Notably a third of them are youths aged between 15 and 24.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some of us have been there before; they are in vacation jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is also useful to consider another group in terms of the existing household support.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Basically, per capita income implies that if you have two persons living in the home, you probably have a household income of more than $2,600.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you have four persons at home, you have household income of more than $5,200 per month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, half of this group have alternative means of support and which also suggests that they are not the primary breadwinners of the household and have other means of support too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In short, of these 30,000 Singaporean employees who still earn less than $1,300 a month today, half of them are staying in households where they are not the primary breadwinners and have others in the household providing income support.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The majority of these 30,000 employees have low education and work as clerks, F&B workers, cleaners and shop salespersons.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And more than one third are older Singaporeans at higher risks of disemployment, while the other one third of them are youths on vacation jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides the monthly Workfare Income Supplement wage top-up they would already receive, this group of 30,000 Singaporeans will continue to be supported by the Workfare Skills Support scheme that will enable them to upskill and earn higher wages, and by other schemes such as the Silver Support, ComCare, GST voucher and U-Save rebates for their daily and medical needs as well as retirement needs in the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Additionally, the Government will continue to raise the standards of living for low-wage workers in other meaningful ways such as providing access to quality healthcare, enhance housing grants and subsidies to help them own their own homes, education for their children and adequate support in retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With all due respect, I wonder if I could get a clarification, specifically with respect to the question, which is that we are wondering how many receive a take-home income of $1,300 and below, excluding all these supplementary schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An alternative way to look at this question is, if we could look at the breakdown of wage earnings only, so what is the share or the number of Singaporeans that receive less than $1,300 based on wage earnings only versus those who receive $1,300 and below, after you take into account all these supplementary schemes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On this, I just want to reiterate that the holistic understanding of Singapore's system, of how we use personal income including CPF and Workfare income payouts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: CPF is part of income too, as these can be used for necessities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare Income Scheme or WIS gives you cash.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As for CPF, I think many of us use it for housing and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think it is worth it to note that 75% of our Workfare recipients, lower income workers, also own their own homes and therefore there is a direct impact from CPF into your home ownership.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is still income which, in other countries, you would have had to use your cash to pay for your own homes or mortgages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In line with the International Labour Organization (ILO) – so this is not a pure Singapore definition – if you think about the alignment, the concept and definition of gross earnings, the data collected is before tax deductions and inclusive of CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you use the ILO statistics of earnings for example, they define to include social security, pension schemes, insurance premiums, union dues and other obligations of the employees.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this is how it is done internationally.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, we keep the same conventions because it provides a meaningful comparisons and benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Calculations to exclude CPF contributions, as asked by the Member, how do you do that?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Or deduction of other incomes will require various other assumptions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For instance, income tax deductions will differ based on individual profiles, and some do get different sorts of reliefs for example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Moreover, almost all the Minimum Wage systems internationally including in the US, UK, Netherlands, Germany, South Korea, Spain also stipulate that Minimum Wages are subject to taxes and social security contributions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That also implies tax as well as social security, your pensions, your CPF.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This means that that Minimum Wage levels are also before deductions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Given this these considerations, it would not be meaningful nor accurate to consider income according to the parameters of the Member's query.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, I would like to turn the question around to the Member and ask for clarification of the Workers' Party's position on the Minimum Wage level that it is advocating for.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Yet, in the September 2020 Debate on the President's Address, Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggest that the appropriate Minimum Wage levels should be – well, he was suggesting that we should have a national commission to determine this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Thereafter, in October 2020, in the Ministerial Statement just last month, Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said that the Workers' Party is proposing a Minimum Wage of $1,300.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Member Mr Pritam Singh also asked Member Mr Edward Chia, if he would be agreeable to pay the 32,000 workers $1,300 as a business employer.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Both these statements suggest a gross Minimum Wage of $1,300 per month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's current query seem to suggest that the Workers' Party is now proposing for a minimum take-home pay of $1,300.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is a shift in where the line is.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because I think it is useful for us to all have this same level of benchmark now, so we can have meaningful debates in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may just quickly expand on the question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I appreciate that the ILO has a particular definition, but I am that he would also appreciate that for a worker who works full-time in Singapore, they will have a notion of how much their labour effort is worth every month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Importantly, to the average Singaporean, what they care about is not necessarily limited to just how much they receive in terms of CPF payments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because, of course, many Singaporeans justifiably think that the CPF payments are what ultimately is what is owed them after all they have saved for that for that amount.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may just step quickly into this Minimum Wage clarification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I should note that the premise of my question had nothing to do with the Minimum Wage per se, the question did not specify anything about Minimum Wage, it was about the idea of $1,300.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, that was in very much, in fact the reason why I had raised this question about $1,300.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the last few debates too, the same figure was mentioned but in different definitions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I think the root of the issue now is the Workers' Party changed its definition for its Minimum Wage line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I do not think I was evading the question because I think the Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad imputed an inference of the $1,300 take-home pay was what the question was asking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think that the Workers' Party's position has been consistent and that it was about $1,300 in terms of full-time work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But this particular question was about take-home pay, in part, because it is about what it means for survival in the case of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is why I do not think that I am actually evading the question because I think that an inference of what I was asking in the question was actually attributed to be, whereas I did not make them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There was a $1,300 gross wage and now he is saying $1,300 take-home.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I appreciate his questions for this Parliamentary Question and I have given the answer as to why you do not separate your CPF, for example, from your salary.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because your CPF clearly provides for amounts of money that you pay for your mortgage and pay for your homes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many of our Workfare recipients, many of our low-income workers own their own homes as a result of the CPF.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To some extent, you have got Government subsidies but you also have CPF flow-through that enables many of our low-income workers to own homes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, that is income too and that is also a recognition by the employer for the ability for workers to earn and that is why we talk about gross wages typically.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Generally, figures are what we pick up from statistics and this is how we do it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is the benchmark, not just by ILO, but Minimum Wage benchmarks around the world too use a similar definition of using tax and social pensions and social security systems as part of the wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If we keep to the convention, it is easier to make for good meaningful benchmarks and discussions and debates, in the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Could I just confirm once again that the Workers' Party's $1,300 Minimum Wage benchmark is gross income, so that we could settle this and come to an understanding.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have a question for Senior Minister of State Zaqy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The question pertains to the age criterion of 35 years old for eligibility for Workfare Income Supplement or WIS.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that this policy's aim is mostly to supplement the income of ageing workers who have a lower chance of increasing their salaries due to their age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Also, the Senior Minister of State Zaqy mentioned about the focus on helping breadwinners of families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The second question is, Senior Minister of State Zaqy mentioned that the amount WIS that an individual gets within a year, ranges from $1,000-plus to a maximum of about $3,600.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Even at the maximum, it translates to about $300 increment on a monthly basis.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From the example here, it does show that we revise and take into account inflation and consider how we can better make Workfare more meaningful for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I can understand the Member's question, in terms of whether we can lower the age criterion and make payouts to those below 35 years old.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But really, the target of WIS and if you look at the profile of those receiving WIS as I had mentioned earlier, more than half are on the older side.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is because the younger workers have got the potential; they are more educated; they have more skills upgrading opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, there is that potential which we want to help through.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But of course, I do understand some are single parents, for example, and some have to take care of family and other issues and have other concerns and challenges in the home.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is where our whole-of-Government efforts come into play – whether it is ComCare for social support, Financial Assistance Schemes in school to help their kids through school too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are ways in which we help them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For worker support, this is where Workfare makes a difference especially for the older workers to beef up and pump up.
